panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Panel a is a plain radiograph of a neonate showing unilateral left femoral deficiency, consistent with the article's diagnosis of isolated unilateral proximal femoral focal deficiency. The panel includes a normal right lower extremity for comparison but clearly demonstrates the left femoral deficiency. [raw subtype: type A] b: Panel b is a follow-up plain radiograph at 18 months showing persistent shortening of the left femur and hypoplastic/shortened femoral head and neck, consistent with proximal femoral focal deficiency. The caption explicitly identifies the left femur, femoral head, and neck abnormalities. [raw subtype: type A]

panels.rationale: Single-panel AP radiograph of both hips at 1 year of age in a case of right proximal femoral focal deficiency. In-text description explicitly identifies pseudarthrosis between the right femoral head and upper femoral shaft, consistent with PFFD; the shortened right femur is also visible. No diagram, control, other disease, or third-party copyright concern. [raw subtype: Aitken type-A or type-B]
panels.attribution_text: Simpson-White et al. King's procedure for Aitken B/Paley 2a proximal femoral focal deficiency with 19-year follow-up--a case report.. Acta orthopaedica 2013. doi:10.3109/17453674.2013.795102. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Both hips at 1 year of age.
in_text_mentions: At the age of 1 year, she underwent a Symes amputation of the right foot and was fitted with a below-knee orthosis, with which she began to walk. During the following year, radiographs suggested a pseudarthrosis between the right femoral head and the upper femoral shaft (Figure 1). Both acetabulae were developing well, with femoral heads enlocated. This was in keeping with an Aitken type-A or type-B PFFD of the right hip (Aitken 1969). The left proximal femur, although not normal, appeared in solid continuity with the femoral head.

reports in the literature [2]. Therefore, for us to have two cases in a short period of less than half a year merits documentation and inclusion in existing literatures. Interestingly, our two patients showed various degrees of involvement, as is known in PFFD [4]. Our first index patient showed severe deficiency of proximal two-thirds of left femur (see Figs. 1 and 2) whereas the second case only showed mild shortening of the left femur (see Figs. 3 and 4). PFFD features are recognized to vary from mild shortening to severe deficiency of the femoral head, acetabulum, and femoral shaft [7, 8].

No skin (only socks, trousers, sweater) is visible so skin tone is null, and no age or ethnicity is stated in the caption/in-text, so age_group is unknown and typicality is atypical per the article's designation of the case as atypical.
